q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Find the longest chain first, then name the branch on it. Is the branch attached at its end carbon or its middle carbon?
w: The longest chain has 7 carbons (heptane). The branch –CH(CH3)2 is attached through its middle carbon, so it is isopropyl, on C4: 4-isopropylheptane. A propyl branch would be –CH2CH2CH3.
x: A propyl branch is a straight –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> attached through its end carbon. Here the branch is attached through its middle carbon, which has a different name.
Recount the longest chain. Running through the branch never gives more than 7 carbons, so the parent is not octane.
A tert-butyl group has four carbons, C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>. Count the carbons in this branch: there are only three.

q: How many primary (1°) carbons are in 2,2,4-trimethylpentane, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CCH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>?
h: A primary carbon is bonded to exactly one other carbon. That means every CH<sub>3</sub> group here.
w: There are three CH3 groups on the quaternary carbon and two on the CH carbon: 5 primary carbons. Answering 2 counts only the two end carbons of the pentane chain and forgets that every branch CH3 is also a 1° carbon. The molecule also has one 2° (CH2), one 3° (CH) and one 4° carbon.
x: 4 misses one CH<sub>3</sub>. Every CH<sub>3</sub> group, whether at a chain end or on a branch, is bonded to just one carbon and counts as 1°.
3 counts only the methyls on the quaternary carbon. The CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the CH carbon are also bonded to only one carbon each.
2 counts only the two ends of the pentane chain. Branch CH<sub>3</sub> groups are also bonded to just one carbon, so they are 1° too.

q: Which compound is a constitutional isomer of hexane?
h: Constitutional isomers have the same molecular formula (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>) but a different connection of atoms.
w: 2,2-Dimethylbutane has 6 C and 14 H, the same as hexane, with a different skeleton, so it is an isomer. Cyclohexane is C6H12; 2-methylhexane is C7H16; 2,2-dimethylpropane is C5H12.
x: Cyclohexane is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>: closing the ring removes 2 H. Isomers must have exactly the same formula as hexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>.
2-Methylhexane has a six-carbon chain plus a methyl: 7 carbons, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub>. An isomer of hexane must have 6 carbons in total.
2,2-Dimethylpropane has only 5 carbons in total (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>). An isomer of hexane needs 6 carbons and 14 H.

q: Which alkene can exist as cis and trans isomers?
h: Each carbon of the double bond must carry two different groups.
w: In 2-pentene each double-bond carbon has an H and a different alkyl group, so CH3CH=CHCH2CH3 has cis and trans forms. The others each have a double-bond carbon with two identical groups (two H or two CH3).
x: The end carbon of CH<sub>2</sub>=CH– carries two H atoms. When one double-bond carbon has two identical groups, swapping sides gives the same molecule.
The left double-bond carbon carries two CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Two identical groups on one C=C carbon rule out cis and trans forms.
Here one C=C carbon has two CH<sub>3</sub> groups and the other has two H atoms, so neither carbon has two different groups.

q: A six-carbon ring has a methyl group on each of two neighboring ring carbons. What is its name?
h: Name the ring by its number of carbons, then number the substituents with the lowest possible numbers.
w: A six-carbon ring is cyclohexane, and neighboring positions are numbered 1 and 2: 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane. 1,3 would skip a carbon; 1,1 would put both methyls on the same carbon.
x: 1,3 would leave one ring carbon between the two methyl groups. Here the methyls are on neighboring carbons.
Cyclopentane is a five-carbon ring. Count the ring carbons in the description again.
1,1 puts both methyl groups on the same ring carbon. Here each methyl is on a different, neighboring carbon.

q: Which alkane has the highest boiling point?
h: Boiling point rises with more carbons and falls with more branching.
w: Hexane has the most carbons and is unbranched, giving the largest surface area and strongest dispersion forces. 2,2-Dimethylbutane has the same formula but is compact, so it boils lower.
x: 2,2-Dimethylbutane has six carbons, but it is compact and highly branched, so it has less surface contact and weaker dispersion forces than an unbranched isomer.
Pentane is unbranched but has only five carbons. A larger molecule here has more electrons and stronger dispersion forces.
2-Methylbutane is small (five carbons) and branched, which both lower the boiling point.

q: Propane burns completely in a gas grill. When the equation below is balanced, what is the coefficient of O<sub>2</sub>?
h: Balance C first, then H, then count the oxygen atoms on the product side.
w: C3H8 + 5 O2 → 3 CO2 + 4 H2O. Products have 3(2) + 4(1) = 10 O atoms, so 5 O2. Choosing 4 copies the water coefficient, 3 copies the CO2 coefficient, and 2 counts only the four O atoms in the water and forgets the six in CO2.
x: 3 copies the CO<sub>2</sub> coefficient. Count all the O atoms in the products: 3 CO<sub>2</sub> plus 4 H<sub>2</sub>O, then divide by 2.
4 copies the H<sub>2</sub>O coefficient. Add up every O atom on the product side, from both CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O, then divide by 2.
2 O<sub>2</sub> supplies only 4 O atoms, enough for the water alone. The CO<sub>2</sub> molecules need oxygen too.

q: Methane reacts with chlorine in the presence of light to form a monochlorinated product. What are the products?
h: In halogenation, one halogen atom replaces one H atom. Where does the removed H go?
w: Substitution swaps one H for one Cl: CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl. The H that leaves combines with the other Cl atom, not with another H.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>Cl is right, but H<sub>2</sub> is not the by-product. The H removed from carbon pairs with the other Cl atom of Cl<sub>2</sub>.
CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> has two H replaced, but the question asks for a monochlorinated product. Also, the removed H leaves with Cl, not as H<sub>2</sub>.
Carbon can form only four bonds, so CH<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> cannot exist. Alkanes have no double bond to add to; a Cl swaps places with an H instead.

q: What is the product when 2-butene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub>, reacts with H<sub>2</sub> over a platinum catalyst?
h: Hydrogenation adds one H to each carbon of the double bond.
w: Adding H2 across the C=C gives CH3CH2CH2CH3, butane. Adding water (hydration) would give 2-butanol instead.
x: 1-Butene is still an alkene: it just moves the C=C. Hydrogenation adds H<sub>2</sub> and removes the double bond entirely.
2-Butanol contains an OH, which would come from adding water (hydration). H<sub>2</sub> supplies only hydrogen atoms.
2-Butyne has a triple bond and fewer H atoms than 2-butene. Hydrogenation adds hydrogen, so the product has more H, not fewer.

q: Propene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub>, reacts with water in the presence of an acid catalyst. What is the major product?
h: Use Markovnikov's rule to decide where the H and the OH go.
w: The H adds to the end CH2 carbon (which already has more H), and the OH adds to the middle carbon, giving 2-propanol, CH3CH(OH)CH3. 1-Propanol would be the anti-Markovnikov product.
x: This puts the OH on the end carbon, which is the anti-Markovnikov product. The H goes to the double-bond carbon that already has more H atoms.
Propane is what H<sub>2</sub> would give. Adding water puts an OH group into the product.
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO is an aldehyde with a C=O. Hydration adds H and OH across the C=C, giving an alcohol, not a carbonyl compound.

q: What is the major product when 2-methylpropene, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH<sub>2</sub>, reacts with HBr?
h: HBr adds H and Br, one to each double-bond carbon. Which carbon gets the H?
w: By Markovnikov's rule, H goes to the CH2 carbon and Br to the carbon bearing the two methyls: (CH3)3CBr, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl bromide). A dibromo product would come from Br2, not HBr.
x: Br on the CH<sub>2</sub> end is the anti-Markovnikov product. The H goes to the double-bond carbon that already has more H atoms.
Two Br atoms would come from Br<sub>2</sub>. HBr adds one H and one Br.
2-Bromobutane has an unbranched four-carbon chain. Addition to the C=C never changes the branched carbon skeleton of 2-methylpropene.

q: Markovnikov's rule states that when HX or H<sub>2</sub>O adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the H atom adds to the double-bond carbon that
c: is bonded to more carbon atoms
is at the center of the chain
h: Remember the phrase: “the rich get richer.”
w: The H goes to the carbon that already has more H atoms, and the X or OH goes to the more substituted carbon. Picking “fewer H” reverses the rule.
x: That reverses the rule. The carbon with fewer H atoms is where the X or OH ends up.
The carbon bonded to more carbons usually has fewer H atoms; that is where X or OH goes, not the H.
Position in the chain does not matter. The rule compares the number of H atoms already on each double-bond carbon.

q: Poly(vinyl chloride), PVC, is used in IV bags and medical tubing. Which monomer is used to make it?
h: An addition polymer is built from an alkene monomer; the name tells you which atom it carries.
w: Vinyl chloride is chloroethene, CH2=CHCl. Ethene makes polyethylene, propene makes polypropylene, and CF2=CF2 makes Teflon.
x: CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub> (ethene) makes polyethylene, which has no chlorine. The name vinyl chloride tells you the monomer carries a Cl.
CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCH<sub>3</sub> (propene) makes polypropylene. The monomer for PVC must contain chlorine.
CF<sub>2</sub>=CF<sub>2</sub> makes Teflon, a fluorine polymer. The monomer for PVC carries chlorine, not fluorine.

q: How many moles of H<sub>2</sub> are needed to completely hydrogenate 1 mole of HC≡C–CH=CH<sub>2</sub>?
h: A C=C uses 1 H<sub>2</sub>; a C≡C uses 2 H<sub>2</sub>.
w: The triple bond needs 2 mol H2 and the double bond needs 1 mol H2: 2 + 1 = 3 mol H2, giving butane. Counting each multiple bond as one gives the tempting answer 2.
x: 2 counts each multiple bond once. A triple bond takes up two H<sub>2</sub> to become a single bond.
1 H<sub>2</sub> would saturate only one pi bond. This molecule has both a C≡C and a C=C to fill.
4 is too many. A triple bond takes two H<sub>2</sub> and a double bond takes one; there is nothing else to add to.

q: Which compound has the molecular formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>?
h: Each ring or double bond removes 2 H from the alkane formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>.
w: Cyclohexene has a ring plus a C=C: 14 − 2 − 2 = 10 H, so C6H10. Cyclohexane and 1-hexene each have only one ring or one double bond (C6H12); hexane is C6H14.
x: Cyclohexane has a ring but no double bond: 14 − 2 = 12 H, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>. Look for a compound with two features that each remove 2 H.
1-Hexene has one C=C and no ring: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>. You need a compound missing 4 H from the alkane formula.
Hexane is the saturated open-chain alkane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>. It has no ring or double bond to remove H atoms.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Number the chain from the end that gives the double bond the lower number.
w: Five carbons with the double bond between C2 and C3 when numbered from the right: 2-pentene. “3-Pentene” comes from numbering from the wrong end.
x: 3-Pentene numbers the chain from the wrong end. Number from the end nearer the double bond so it gets the lowest number.
Count the carbons: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> has five, so the parent is pentene, not hexene.
1-Pentene has the C=C at the end of the chain. Here the double bond is between two inner carbons.

q: Heating 1-propanol with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> gives propene, as shown below. This elimination is called
h: Name the small molecule removed: H<sub>2</sub>, HX, H<sub>2</sub>O or X<sub>2</sub>.
w: An H and an –OH are removed from neighboring carbons as H2O, forming C=C: dehydration. Hydration is the reverse (adding water to an alkene).
x: Dehydrogenation removes H<sub>2</sub>. Here an alcohol loses its –OH along with an H, so the small molecule removed contains oxygen.
Dehydrohalogenation removes H and a halogen (HX). 1-Propanol has no halogen atom.
Hydration adds water to an alkene. This reaction goes the other way: water is removed from an alcohol to make an alkene.

q: Propene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub>, reacts with HBr to give 2-bromopropane, CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub>. Why is this classified as an addition reaction?
c: The H and Br add across the C=C, and no atoms are lost: two reactants give one product
A Br atom replaces an H atom, and HBr is released
Atoms are removed from neighboring carbons to form a C=C
The alkene reacts with O<sub>2</sub> to give CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O
h: Compare the reactants and products. Did the C=C form, break, or stay? Was anything left over?
w: In an addition reaction the parts of a reagent add to the two carbons of a C=C, which becomes a single bond. Here H and Br add across the C=C and nothing is lost, so two reactants give one product. (Markovnikov's rule puts the H on CH2 and the Br on the middle carbon.)
x: That describes a substitution, such as the halogenation of an alkane in light. Here no H atom is replaced and no HBr is released; HBr is used up.
That describes an elimination, which forms a C=C. Here the C=C is used up.
That describes combustion. This reaction uses HBr, not O<sub>2</sub>.

q: Which reactant gives propene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub>, when it is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (dehydration)?
h: Dehydration removes H<sub>2</sub>O, so the reactant needs an –OH group.
w: Dehydration removes an –OH and an H from neighboring carbons as H2O, forming a C=C. 2-Propanol, CH3CH(OH)CH3, loses water to give propene. This elimination is the reverse of the hydration of propene.
x: This compound has no –OH group, so it cannot lose H<sub>2</sub>O.
Propane has no –OH group to lose as water. Alkanes do not undergo dehydration.
Propanal is an aldehyde. Its oxygen is in a C=O, not an –OH, so it does not lose water to form an alkene.

q: Ethanol is heated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and gives ethene, as shown below. What is removed, and what is the reaction called?
h: Compare formulas: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>. What is missing?
w: C2H6O minus C2H4 leaves H2O, so water is removed and a C=C forms: dehydration, an elimination reaction. Hydration is the reverse addition of water to an alkene.
x: Removing only H<sub>2</sub> would leave the oxygen behind in the product. The product, ethene, has no oxygen.
Hydration adds water to an alkene. Here water is removed from an alcohol, so the name needs a prefix meaning removal.
In a substitution one group replaces another and no C=C forms. Here a C=C forms and a water molecule leaves.

q: Which condensed structure is the isobutyl group?
h: Iso- names a chain ending in a carbon with two CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Where is the attachment point relative to that branch?
w: Isobutyl is attached through a CH2 to a Y-shaped CH(CH3)2: –CH2CH(CH3)2. The others are sec-butyl, tert-butyl and butyl.
x: This is sec-butyl: it attaches through a CH that carries a CH<sub>3</sub> and an ethyl. In iso- groups the Y-shaped CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> is at the far end.
This is tert-butyl: it attaches through a carbon bonded to three CH<sub>3</sub> groups.
This is the unbranched butyl group. Iso- groups end in a branch with two CH<sub>3</sub> groups.

q: What is the common name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHClCH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Find the carbon bonded to Cl. How many other carbons is it bonded to?
w: Cl is on carbon 2 of a straight 4-carbon chain; that carbon is bonded to two carbons (secondary): sec-butyl chloride (2-chlorobutane). Butyl chloride has Cl on the end carbon; isobutyl and tert-butyl are branched.
x: Isobutyl compounds have a branched chain, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>–. This four-carbon chain is unbranched.
In tert-butyl chloride the Cl carbon is bonded to three other carbons. Here the Cl carbon is bonded to only two.
Butyl chloride has Cl on the end carbon of the chain. Here the Cl is on an inner carbon.

q: Propene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub>, reacts with Br<sub>2</sub>, decolorizing the red-brown bromine. What is the product?
h: Halogenation opens the double bond and adds one halogen atom to each of the two double-bond carbons.
w: One Br adds to each former C=C carbon: CH3CHBrCH2Br (1,2-dibromopropane). The single-Br products come from HBr (hydrohalogenation), not Br2.
x: This has only one Br, on the end carbon. Br<sub>2</sub> supplies two Br atoms, one for each double-bond carbon.
This has only one Br, which is what HBr would give. Br<sub>2</sub> adds a Br to each of the two double-bond carbons.
Both Br atoms are on the same carbon here. In halogenation each carbon of the C=C gets one Br.

q: Three of these alkenes give 2-methylbutane when H<sub>2</sub> adds over a Pt catalyst. Which alkene gives a different alkane?
h: Hydrogenation adds H to each C=C carbon but never changes the carbon skeleton. Which choice does not have a branched four-carbon chain?
w: H2 only saturates the C=C; the skeleton stays the same. The three branched alkenes all have a CH3 on carbon 2 of a four-carbon chain, so each gives 2-methylbutane. CH2=CHCH2CH2CH3 (1-pentene) is unbranched and gives pentane instead.
x: CH<sub>2</sub>=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has a CH<sub>3</sub> branch on carbon 2 of a four-carbon chain, so H<sub>2</sub> turns it into 2-methylbutane. Look for a skeleton without a branch.
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CHCH<sub>3</sub> is branched; saturating its C=C gives 2-methylbutane. Look for a skeleton without a branch.
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH=CH<sub>2</sub> is branched; saturating its C=C gives 2-methylbutane. Look for a skeleton without a branch.

q: Bromine is red-brown. When Br<sub>2</sub> is added to 1-butene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, the color disappears. Which compound forms?
h: Halogenation of an alkene is an addition: open the double bond and put one Br on each of its two carbons.
w: Br–Br adds across the C=C, one Br on each double-bond carbon: CH2BrCHBrCH2CH3 (1,2-dibromobutane). CH3CHBrCH2CH3 would come from HBr, not Br2.
x: This has only one Br, on C2: that is the HBr product. Br<sub>2</sub> adds two Br atoms.
This has only one Br. Br<sub>2</sub> supplies two Br atoms, one for each carbon of the C=C.
This puts a Br on C3, which was not part of the double bond. Both Br atoms go on the two carbons of the C=C.

q: Predict the alcohol formed in greatest amount when H<sub>2</sub>O (acid catalyst) adds to (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CHCH<sub>3</sub>, 2-methyl-2-butene.
h: Hydration adds H and OH across the C=C. Markovnikov: the H goes to the double-bond carbon that already has more H atoms.
w: The C=C carbons are C2 (no H) and C3 (one H). H adds to C3 and OH adds to C2, giving (CH3)2C(OH)CH2CH3 (2-methyl-2-butanol). Putting OH on C3 is the anti-Markovnikov mistake.
x: This puts the OH on C3, the double-bond carbon that had an H: the anti-Markovnikov product. The OH goes to the carbon with fewer H atoms.
The OH here is on C4, a carbon that was not part of the C=C. Hydration only adds to the two double-bond carbons.
This alkane has no OH; it is what H<sub>2</sub> would give. Water adds an H and an OH.

q: 1-Butene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub>, reacts with HI to give 2-iodobutane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHICH<sub>3</sub>. Which type of reaction is this?
h: Look at what added across the double bond: H<sub>2</sub>, X<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O or H–X?
w: An H and an I (from H–I) added across the C=C, so this is hydrohalogenation, an addition reaction. Halogenation would add two halogen atoms (X2); dehydrohalogenation is the reverse, removing H–X to make an alkene.
x: Halogenation adds X<sub>2</sub>, putting a halogen on both carbons. Here an H and only one I were added.
That name describes removing H and a halogen to make an alkene. Here something was added to the alkene, not removed.
Hydrogenation adds H<sub>2</sub>, giving an alkane with no I. Look at what actually added across the double bond.

q: An alkyne has the condensed formula CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C≡CCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>. Which name is correct?
h: Give the triple bond the lowest number first. If that is a tie, number so the branch gets the lower number.
w: The chain has 6 carbons and the C≡C starts at C3 from either end, so the tie is broken by the branch: numbering from the isopropyl end puts the CH3 on C2: 2-methyl-3-hexyne. 5-Methyl gives the branch a higher number, and "-ene" would mean a C=C.
x: 5-Methyl numbers from the wrong end. The triple bond gets C3 either way, so the tie goes to the numbering that gives the branch the lower number.
-Ene means a C=C double bond. This molecule has a C≡C triple bond, which uses the -yne ending.
4-Hexyne gives the triple bond a higher number than needed. Number from the end that gives the C≡C the lowest number.

q: A branched alkane has the condensed formula CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. Which name follows IUPAC rules?
h: Find the longest chain, number from the end nearest the first branch, and list substituents alphabetically.
w: The longest chain has 6 carbons. Numbering from the left puts branches at C2 (methyl) and C4 (ethyl); from the right they would be 3 and 5. Alphabetical order (ethyl before methyl) gives 4-ethyl-2-methylhexane.
x: The numbers are right, but substituents must be listed in alphabetical order. Compare the first letters of ethyl and methyl.
3 and 5 come from numbering from the end farther from the first branch. Number from the end that reaches a branch first.
An ethyl group on C2 means the chain was not the longest one: that ethyl would extend the main chain. Also check which end is nearer the first branch.

q: Light shines on a mixture of cyclohexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, and Br<sub>2</sub>. Which set of products forms?
h: An alkane has no double bond to open, so in light a halogen can only swap places with one H.
w: Alkanes undergo substitution: one H is replaced by Br, and that H leaves with the other Br as HBr: C6H11Br + HBr. Adding Br2 across a bond only happens with alkenes.
x: Br<sub>2</sub> cannot add to an alkane: there is no double bond to open. In light, a Br replaces an H instead.
The H removed from carbon pairs with the other Br atom, not with another H. Also, one Br<sub>2</sub> replaces only one H.
C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>11</sub>Br is right, but the H that leaves does not form H<sub>2</sub>. It combines with the second Br atom of Br<sub>2</sub>.

q: Octane is a major component of gasoline. When the equation below for its complete combustion is balanced with the smallest whole numbers, what is the coefficient of O<sub>2</sub>?
h: Balance C, then H, then O. If O<sub>2</sub> needs a half, double every coefficient.
w: C8H18 → 8 CO2 + 9 H2O needs 8(2) + 9 = 25 O atoms = 12.5 O2. Doubling everything gives 2 C8H18 + 25 O2 → 16 CO2 + 18 H2O. Answering 12.5 stops before doubling, which is not a whole number; 16 copies the CO2 coefficient; 17 adds 8 + 9.
x: 12.5 balances the atoms, but it is not a whole number. Double every coefficient so all of them are whole numbers.
17 adds the CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O coefficients (8 + 9). Count O atoms instead: 2 per CO<sub>2</sub> and 1 per H<sub>2</sub>O, then divide by 2.
16 copies the CO<sub>2</sub> coefficient after doubling. The O<sub>2</sub> coefficient comes from counting every O atom in the products.

q: Name this alkene, in which the CH<sub>3</sub> group and the propyl group lie on opposite sides of the C=C: CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.
h: Same side = cis, opposite sides = trans. Then number the chain so the C=C gets the lowest number.
w: The six-carbon chain is numbered from the end nearer the C=C, so the double bond starts at C2, and groups on opposite sides are trans: trans-2-hexene. Numbering from the other end (4-hexene) gives a higher number, and "hexyne" would mean a triple bond, which cannot be cis or trans.
x: Cis means the two carbon groups are on the same side of the C=C. In this molecule they are on opposite sides.
4-Hexene numbers from the end farther from the double bond. Number so the C=C gets the lowest number.
Hexyne means a C≡C triple bond. This compound has a C=C double bond; a triple bond cannot have cis or trans forms.

q: 2-Methyl-1-butene reacts with HCl as shown below. Predict the major organic product.
h: Hydrogen wants to make the most friends: H goes to the C=C carbon that already has more H atoms.
w: C1 (=CH2) has two H and C2 has none, so H adds to C1 and Cl adds to C2: CH3CCl(CH3)CH2CH3, 2-chloro-2-methylbutane. 1-Chloro-2-methylbutane is the anti-Markovnikov product; a dichloride would need Cl2.
x: Cl on C1 is the anti-Markovnikov product. C1 already has two H, so it gets the new H; Cl goes to the other double-bond carbon.
This puts the Cl next to the branch, on a carbon that was not part of the C=C. HCl adds only to the two double-bond carbons.
Two Cl atoms would need Cl<sub>2</sub>. HCl adds one H and one Cl.

q: The alkene shown reacts with H<sub>2</sub> over a platinum catalyst. What is the product?
h: Hydrogenation adds one H to each carbon of the C=C. Nothing else in the molecule changes.
w: H2 adds across the C=C, giving methylcyclohexane: the ring and the methyl group stay in place. The aromatic ring (toluene) would need H2 to be removed; the alcohol would need water (hydration); the open chain would need the ring to break.
x: This is toluene, an aromatic ring with fewer H atoms than the reactant. Making it would require removing H<sub>2</sub>, not adding it.
This is an alcohol with an OH group, which would come from adding water. H<sub>2</sub> supplies only hydrogen atoms.
This is an open seven-carbon chain. Hydrogenation does not break the ring; it only adds H across the C=C.

q: Sorbic acid, a food preservative, is treated with excess H<sub>2</sub> and a nickel catalyst. What is the product?
h: Excess H<sub>2</sub> saturates every C=C. Under these conditions the C=O of a carboxylic acid is not reduced.
w: Both C=C double bonds take up H2 (2 H2 total), giving hexanoic acid. Keeping one C=C means only one H2 was added. The carboxyl group (COOH) is not reduced by H2/Ni, so the aldehyde and the alcohol are wrong.
x: This structure still has one C=C, so only one H<sub>2</sub> was added. Excess H<sub>2</sub> saturates every C=C.
This is an alcohol: the COOH group has been reduced to CH<sub>2</sub>OH. H<sub>2</sub>/Ni does not reduce a carboxylic acid group.
This is an aldehyde: the COOH group has lost an O. H<sub>2</sub>/Ni does not change the carboxylic acid group.

q: Cyclopentene reacts with Cl<sub>2</sub> as shown. What is the product?
h: In halogenation, one halogen atom adds to each carbon of the double bond.
w: The Cl–Cl adds across the C=C: one Cl on each of the two former double-bond carbons, giving 1,2-dichlorocyclopentane. A single Cl would come from HCl, not Cl2. Putting both Cl on one carbon, or on carbons that were not part of the C=C, is not addition across the double bond.
x: This has only one Cl, which is what HCl would give. Cl<sub>2</sub> adds two Cl atoms.
Here the two Cl atoms are on carbons with a CH<sub>2</sub> between them. Only neighboring carbons were joined by the C=C.
Both Cl atoms are on the same carbon. In halogenation each carbon of the C=C gets one Cl.

q: 3-Methyl-1-butene, shown, reacts with Br<sub>2</sub>. What is the product?
h: Br<sub>2</sub> adds one Br to each carbon that was in the C=C. Find those two carbons first.
w: The C=C is between C1 and C2, so Br adds to both: 1,2-dibromo-3-methylbutane. The structures with only one Br come from HBr, not Br2. Placing a Br on C3 puts it on a carbon that was not part of the double bond.
x: This has only one Br, on C2: that is what HBr would give. Br<sub>2</sub> adds two Br atoms.
This puts a Br on C3, the carbon carrying the methyl. C3 was not part of the C=C.
This has only one Br, on the end carbon. Br<sub>2</sub> supplies a Br for each of the two double-bond carbons.

q: 2-Methyl-2-butene, shown, reacts with HBr. What is the major product?
h: Markovnikov's rule: the H goes to the double-bond carbon that already has more H atoms.
w: The C=C carbons are C2 (no H) and C3 (one H). H adds to C3 and Br adds to the more substituted C2: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane. Br on C3 is the anti-Markovnikov product. Two Br atoms would need Br2, and an OH would need water.
x: This puts Br on the double-bond carbon that had an H: the anti-Markovnikov product. Br goes to the carbon with fewer H atoms.
This has two Br atoms, which would require Br<sub>2</sub>. HBr adds one H and one Br.
This has an OH group, which would come from water. HBr adds an H and a Br.

q: 2-Methylpropene, shown, reacts with HCl. What is the major product?
h: Markovnikov's rule: the H adds to the C=C carbon with more H atoms; Cl ends up on the other carbon.
w: H adds to the CH2 end and Cl to the carbon bearing the two methyl groups, giving tert-butyl chloride (2-chloro-2-methylpropane). Cl on the CH2 end (isobutyl chloride) is the anti-Markovnikov product; two Cl atoms would need Cl2.
x: This puts Cl on the CH<sub>2</sub> end: the anti-Markovnikov product. The CH<sub>2</sub> carbon has more H, so it receives the H.
This has two Cl atoms, which would require Cl<sub>2</sub>. HCl adds one H and one Cl.
This has an OH group, which would come from water. HCl adds an H and a Cl.

q: 1-Butene, shown, reacts with water in the presence of an acid catalyst (H+). What is the major product?
h: Hydration adds H and OH across the C=C and follows Markovnikov's rule.
w: H adds to C1 (the CH2 end, more H) and OH adds to C2, giving 2-butanol. 1-Butanol is the anti-Markovnikov product; the diol adds OH to both carbons; butane comes from adding H2, not water.
x: This puts the OH on C1, the CH<sub>2</sub> end: the anti-Markovnikov product. C1 has more H, so it receives the H.
This diol has two OH groups. Water adds one H and one OH across the C=C.
Butane has no OH; it is what H<sub>2</sub> would give. Water adds an H and an OH.

q: 1-Methylcyclopentene, shown, is heated with H2O and H2SO4 (acid catalyst). What is the major product?
h: Markovnikov's rule: the OH goes to the double-bond carbon that has fewer H atoms.
w: The ring carbon bearing the methyl group has no H; the other C=C carbon has one H. H adds to the CH carbon and OH to the methyl-bearing carbon: 1-methylcyclopentanol, a tertiary alcohol. 2-Methylcyclopentanol is the anti-Markovnikov product.
x: This puts the OH on the ring carbon that had an H: the anti-Markovnikov product. The OH goes to the double-bond carbon with fewer H atoms.
This diol has two OH groups. Water adds one H and one OH across the C=C.
This has no OH; it is what H<sub>2</sub> would give. Water adds an H and an OH.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the alkane shown?
h: Find the longest continuous chain first (it may bend), then number from the end nearer the first branch. List substituents alphabetically.
w: The longest chain has 6 carbons (hexane). Numbering from the end nearer the branches gives a methyl on C2 and an ethyl on C4: 4-ethyl-2-methylhexane (ethyl before methyl alphabetically). "Heptane" miscounts the chain; the other names put the branches on the wrong carbons.
x: Recount the longest chain carefully. Following the bends gives 6 carbons, not 7, whichever path you take.
An ethyl group on C2 means the chain is not the longest: the ethyl would extend it. Find the longest chain first, then number.
3-Ethyl-2-methyl puts the branches on neighboring carbons. In this structure a CH<sub>2</sub> sits between the two branch points.

q: What is the name of the alkene drawn?
h: Number the chain so the double bond gets the lowest number, then check whether the chain continues on the same or opposite sides.
w: Numbering from the end nearer the C=C puts it at C2 (never "3-pentene"). The CH3 and the CH2CH3 are on opposite sides, so it is trans-2-pentene. Choosing cis comes from looking at the H atoms (not drawn) instead of the carbon chain.
x: Cis means the carbon chain continues on the same side of the C=C. Follow the CH<sub>3</sub> and the CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>: which sides are they on?
3-Pentene numbers from the wrong end. Number from the end nearer the C=C.
This numbers from the wrong end; a C=C in pentene is never at 3. Also check which sides the two carbon groups are on.

q: cis-3-Hexen-1-ol gives freshly cut grass its smell. The hydrocarbon part is drawn below without the OH. What is its name?
h: Count the carbons, number from the end nearer the C=C, and see whether the two ethyl groups are on the same side.
w: Six carbons, C=C between C3 and C4 (the same from either end), and both CH2CH3 groups on the same side: cis-3-hexene. Trans would put them on opposite sides (a straight zig-zag); 2-hexene would need the C=C one carbon closer to an end.
x: Trans would put the two ethyl groups on opposite sides of the C=C. Look at the drawing: which side is each ethyl on?
2-Hexene would have a CH<sub>3</sub> directly on one double-bond carbon. Here each double-bond carbon carries an ethyl group.
Count the carbons: there are six, so the parent is hexene, not heptene.

q: Which hydrocarbon has the highest boiling point?
h: All four are nonpolar. Which has the most carbons (the most electrons for London dispersion forces)?
w: 2-Hexene has six carbons, the most electrons and the largest surface, so it has the strongest London dispersion forces (bp about 68 °C). 1-Pentyne (40 °C), 1,3-butadiene (−4 °C) and propene (−48 °C) are smaller. The number or type of double and triple bonds matters much less than the size of the molecule.
x: 1-Pentyne has only five carbons. A triple bond barely changes the boiling point; molecular size matters much more.
1,3-Butadiene has only four carbons. Having two double bonds does not make up for its small size.
Propene has only three carbons, so its dispersion forces are very weak; it is a gas at room temperature.

q: Cyclohexene quickly decolorizes a red-brown solution of Br<sub>2</sub>. What is the product of the reaction shown?
h: Halogenation of an alkene is an addition: the Br–Br bond breaks and one Br adds to each carbon of the C=C.
w: One Br adds to each carbon of the C=C, giving 1,2-dibromocyclohexane (the color disappears because Br2 is used up). Bromocyclohexane has only one Br, which is what HBr would give. In the 1,1- and 1,3-isomers a Br sits on a carbon that was never part of the double bond.
x: This has only one Br, which is what HBr would give. Br<sub>2</sub> adds two Br atoms.
Both Br atoms are on the same carbon. In halogenation each carbon of the C=C gets one Br.
Here the two Br atoms have a CH<sub>2</sub> between them, so one sits on a carbon that was never part of the C=C.

q: What is the major product of the reaction of 1-methylcyclohexene shown?
h: Markovnikov's rule: the H adds to the C=C carbon that already has more H atoms; Br goes to the other carbon.
w: The ring carbon holding the CH3 has no H; the other C=C carbon has one H. H adds to the CH carbon and Br to the carbon with the methyl group: 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane. 1-Bromo-2-methylcyclohexane is the anti-Markovnikov product. Two Br atoms would need Br2, and an OH would need water.
x: This puts Br on the ring carbon that had an H: the anti-Markovnikov product. Br goes to the double-bond carbon with fewer H atoms.
This has two Br atoms, which would require Br<sub>2</sub>. HBr adds one H and one Br.
This has an OH group, which would come from water. HBr adds an H and a Br.

q: What is the product of the reaction of 4-methyl-2-pentyne shown?
h: Two H<sub>2</sub> add across a C≡C, two H atoms on each carbon. Hydrogenation never moves a branch.
w: Two H2 saturate the triple bond, and the carbon skeleton is unchanged: 2-methylpentane. The alkene (4-methyl-2-pentene) is what one H2 gives. Hexane and 2,3-dimethylbutane have the same formula, C6H14, but their carbon skeletons differ from the reactant, and H2 cannot rearrange carbons.
x: This alkene still has a C=C, so only one H<sub>2</sub> was added. Two H<sub>2</sub> fully saturate the triple bond.
Hexane is unbranched, so the branch has been lost. Hydrogenation never changes the carbon skeleton.
2,3-Dimethylbutane has a different carbon skeleton from the reactant. H<sub>2</sub> cannot move carbon atoms around.

q: Limonene gives oranges their scent. What is the product of the reaction shown?
h: Count the C=C bonds. Excess H<sub>2</sub> adds to every one of them.
w: Limonene has two C=C bonds and excess H2 adds to both (2 H2), giving 1-isopropyl-4-methylcyclohexane. The two structures that still have one C=C show only one H2 added. The benzene ring structure has fewer H atoms than limonene, so it would need H2 removed, not added.
x: The ring C=C is still there; only the side-chain C=C was saturated. Excess H<sub>2</sub> adds to every C=C.
The side-chain C=C is still there; only the ring was saturated. Excess H<sub>2</sub> adds to every C=C.
This benzene ring has fewer H atoms than limonene. Adding H<sub>2</sub> increases the H count, so it cannot form an aromatic ring.

q: Which alkene gives 1-chloro-1-ethylcyclohexane, shown, as the major product when it reacts with HCl?
h: Work backward: the Cl sits on a carbon that was part of the C=C, and by Markovnikov's rule it was the C=C carbon with fewer H atoms.
w: In 1-ethylcyclohexene the ring carbon holding the ethyl group has no H, so H adds to its neighbor and Cl adds to the ethyl-bearing carbon, giving the product shown. In 3- and 4-ethylcyclohexene the C=C carbons have no ethyl group, so the Cl cannot end up on the ethyl-bearing carbon. Vinylcyclohexane puts Cl on the side chain: 1-chloro-1-cyclohexylethane.
x: In 3-ethylcyclohexene the C=C carbons do not carry the ethyl group. HCl adds only to the C=C carbons, so the Cl could not land on the ethyl-bearing carbon.
Here the C=C is in the side chain, not the ring. HCl would put the Cl on the side-chain carbon next to the ring, not on a ring carbon.
In 4-ethylcyclohexene the C=C is on the far side of the ring from the ethyl group, so Cl would end up on a different ring carbon.

q: What is the major product of the reaction of 2-methyl-2-pentene shown?
h: Hydration adds H and OH across the C=C. The OH goes on the C=C carbon with fewer H atoms.
w: C2 (bonded to two CH3 groups) has no H and C3 has one H, so H adds to C3 and OH to C2: 2-methyl-2-pentanol, a 3° alcohol. 2-Methyl-3-pentanol is the anti-Markovnikov product. 2-Methylpentane comes from H2, not water, and the diol adds two OH groups.
x: This puts the OH on C3, the double-bond carbon that had an H: the anti-Markovnikov product. The OH goes to the carbon with fewer H atoms.
This alkane has no OH; it is what H<sub>2</sub> would give. Water adds an H and an OH.
This diol has two OH groups. Water adds one H and one OH across the C=C.

q: Styrene is used to make polystyrene. What is the major product of the reaction shown?
h: Only the C=C outside the ring reacts. Apply Markovnikov's rule to its two carbons.
w: The CH2 end of the C=C has more H, so it gets the H and Br goes to the carbon attached to the ring: 1-bromo-1-phenylethane. Br on the CH2 end is the anti-Markovnikov product. The benzene ring does not add HBr, and putting Br on the ring would need Br2 with FeBr3. Two Br atoms would need Br2.
x: This puts Br on the CH<sub>2</sub> end: the anti-Markovnikov product. The CH<sub>2</sub> carbon has more H, so it receives the H.
Here the C=C is untouched and a Br has replaced a ring H. HBr adds across the alkene C=C; the aromatic ring does not react.
This has two Br atoms, which would require Br<sub>2</sub>. HBr adds one H and one Br.

q: What is the product of the reaction of 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene shown?
h: H<sub>2</sub> adds one H to each carbon of the C=C. The methyl groups stay where they are.
w: H2 adds across the C=C, giving 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane; both methyl groups stay on neighboring carbons. 1,1-Dimethylcyclohexane moves a methyl group. The aromatic ring (1,2-dimethylbenzene) has fewer H atoms, and the alcohol would come from hydration, not H2.
x: This is an aromatic ring with fewer H atoms than the reactant. H<sub>2</sub> adds hydrogen, so the product has more H, not fewer.
Here both methyl groups are on the same carbon, so a methyl has moved. Hydrogenation does not move groups.
This has an OH group, which would come from water. H<sub>2</sub> supplies only hydrogen atoms.

q: What is the product of the reaction of trans-2-pentene shown?
h: Find the two carbons of the C=C. In halogenation, one Cl adds to each of them.
w: The C=C is between C2 and C3, so Cl adds to both: 2,3-dichloropentane. 2-Chloropentane has only one Cl, which HCl would give. 3,3-Dichloropentane puts both Cl on one carbon, and 1,2-dichloropentane uses C1, which was not part of the double bond.
x: This has only one Cl, which is what HCl would give. Cl<sub>2</sub> adds two Cl atoms.
Both Cl atoms are on the same carbon. In halogenation each carbon of the C=C gets one Cl.
This puts a Cl on C1, the CH<sub>3</sub> end. C1 was not part of the C=C.

q: What is the major product of the reaction of 1-hexene shown?
h: Markovnikov's rule: the H adds to the C=C carbon that already has more H atoms.
w: C1 (CH2) has more H than C2 (CH), so H adds to C1 and Cl to C2: 2-chlorohexane. 1-Chlorohexane is the anti-Markovnikov product. 1,2-Dichlorohexane would need Cl2, and 3-chlorohexane puts Cl on a carbon that was not in the C=C.
x: This puts Cl on C1, the CH<sub>2</sub> end: the anti-Markovnikov product. C1 has more H, so it receives the H.
This has two Cl atoms, which would require Cl<sub>2</sub>. HCl adds one H and one Cl.
This puts Cl on C3, which was not part of the C=C. HCl adds only to the two double-bond carbons.

q: What is the product of the reaction of 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene shown?
h: Br<sub>2</sub> adds one Br to each carbon of the C=C, even when those carbons are crowded with methyl groups.
w: Each C=C carbon gets one Br: 2,3-dibromo-2,3-dimethylbutane. The single-Br product comes from HBr. Putting a Br on a CH3 group uses a carbon outside the double bond, and 2,3-dimethylbutane is the H2 product.
x: This has only one Br, which is what HBr would give. Br<sub>2</sub> adds two Br atoms.
One Br here is on a CH<sub>3</sub> group, a carbon outside the double bond. Each Br goes on a carbon of the C=C.
This alkane has no Br; it is what H<sub>2</sub> would give.

q: What is the major product of the reaction of methylenecyclohexane shown?
h: One C=C carbon is CH<sub>2</sub> and the other is in the ring with no H. Which one gets the OH?
w: The CH2 end has more H, so it takes the H and becomes a CH3; the OH goes to the ring carbon: 1-methylcyclohexanol. Cyclohexylmethanol is the anti-Markovnikov product. 2-Methylcyclohexanol puts the OH on a ring carbon that was not part of the C=C, and methylcyclohexane would come from H2.
x: This puts the OH on the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon outside the ring: the anti-Markovnikov product. The CH<sub>2</sub> end has more H, so it receives the H.
Here the OH is on a ring carbon next to the one that was in the C=C. Hydration only adds to the two double-bond carbons.
This has no OH; it is what H<sub>2</sub> would give. Water adds an H and an OH.

q: What is the major product of the reaction of 2-ethyl-1-butene shown?
h: Markovnikov's rule: Cl ends up on the C=C carbon with fewer H atoms.
w: C1 (=CH2) gets the H and becomes CH3; Cl goes to C2, which holds the two ethyl groups: 3-chloro-3-methylpentane. 1-Chloro-2-ethylbutane is the anti-Markovnikov product. The alcohol needs water, and the dichloride needs Cl2.
x: This puts Cl on the CH<sub>2</sub> end: the anti-Markovnikov product. The CH<sub>2</sub> carbon has more H, so it receives the H.
This has an OH group, which would come from water. HCl adds an H and a Cl.
This has two Cl atoms, which would require Cl<sub>2</sub>. HCl adds one H and one Cl.

q: Which reagent carries out the conversion shown?
h: The product has one Cl and the C=C is gone. Which reagent adds H to one carbon and Cl to the other?
w: Hydrohalogenation with HCl adds H to one C=C carbon and Cl to the other, giving chlorocyclohexane. Cl2 (with or without FeCl3) adds a Cl to both carbons, giving 1,2-dichlorocyclohexane. Aqueous NaCl only supplies Cl− ions, which do not add to an alkene.
x: Cl<sub>2</sub> adds a Cl to both carbons of the C=C, giving a dichloride. The product here has only one Cl, and an H was added too.
FeCl<sub>3</sub> is the catalyst for substituting Cl onto a benzene ring. With an alkene, Cl<sub>2</sub> still puts a Cl on both C=C carbons.
Aqueous NaCl provides only Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions; it has no H to add and does not react with an alkene.

q: A hydrocarbon is labeled saturated. What must be true of its structure?
c: It contains only C–C and C–H single bonds, so it cannot add H<sub>2</sub>.
It contains at least one C=C double bond, so it can add H<sub>2</sub>.
It contains as many double bonds as the carbon skeleton allows.
It is a hydrocarbon that dissolves readily in water.
h: "Saturated" means the molecule is already full of hydrogen: no more can be added.
w: A saturated hydrocarbon (an alkane or cycloalkane) has only single bonds; every carbon already holds the maximum number of H atoms, so it cannot undergo addition. Compounds with C=C or C≡C are unsaturated and can add H2. Solubility in water has nothing to do with saturation; hydrocarbons of both kinds are insoluble.
x: A C=C double bond makes a hydrocarbon unsaturated, able to add H<sub>2</sub>. Saturated means the opposite.
Many double bonds would make it highly unsaturated. Saturated means it already holds all the H it can.
Saturation describes bonding, not solubility. Hydrocarbons, saturated or not, are nonpolar and insoluble in water.

q: Only one of the drawn hydrocarbons is saturated. Pick it.
h: Saturated = no double or triple bonds anywhere, ring or chain.
w: Methylcyclopentane has only single bonds, so it is saturated; a ring by itself does not count as unsaturation in this sense. 1-Pentene (C=C), 2-pentyne (C≡C) and benzene (alternating double bonds) are all unsaturated and can take up H2.
x: This chain has a C=C double bond, so it is unsaturated and can add H<sub>2</sub>.
This chain has a C≡C triple bond, so it is unsaturated and can add H<sub>2</sub>.
This is benzene, drawn with alternating double bonds, so it is unsaturated. Look for a structure with only single bonds.

q: Cyclohexene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>, reacts with H<sub>2</sub> over a platinum catalyst. What is the product?
h: Hydrogenation adds one H<sub>2</sub> across each C=C. Does the ring open?
w: H2 adds across the one C=C, giving the saturated ring cyclohexane, C6H12. The ring stays closed.
x: Benzene has fewer H atoms than cyclohexene. Hydrogenation adds hydrogen; it does not remove it.
Hexane is an open chain. Hydrogenation adds H<sub>2</sub> to the C=C but does not break the ring.
Cyclohexanol would come from adding H<sub>2</sub>O (hydration), not H<sub>2</sub>.

q: Which alkene gives 2-methyl-2-propanol, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COH, as the major product when it reacts with H<sub>2</sub>O and an acid catalyst?
h: Work backward. The –OH is on a carbon bonded to three CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Which alkene has that branched skeleton?
w: Hydration does not change the carbon skeleton. Only 2-methylpropene has the branched four-carbon skeleton, and by Markovnikov's rule the H adds to the CH2 and the –OH goes to the carbon with the two CH3 groups, giving (CH3)3COH.
x: 1-Butene has an unbranched chain. Its major hydration product is 2-butanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.
2-Butene is unbranched and gives 2-butanol. The product here has a branched skeleton.
Propene has only three carbons and gives 2-propanol. The product here has four carbons.

q: Which alkene reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> to give 2,3-dibromobutane, CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCHBrCH<sub>3</sub>?
h: In halogenation of an alkene, the two Br atoms add to the two carbons that were joined by the C=C.
w: The Br atoms end up on C2 and C3, so the C=C was between C2 and C3: 2-butene. Addition of Br2 is the reaction behind the bromine test, in which the red-brown color disappears.
x: 1-Butene has its C=C between C1 and C2, so it gives 1,2-dibromobutane.
Butane has no C=C, so Br<sub>2</sub> cannot add to it. In light it would undergo substitution and give a single Br plus HBr.
2-Methylpropene has a branched skeleton and gives 1,2-dibromo-2-methylpropane, not an unbranched product.

q: Which of the following reactions is a substitution?
h: In a substitution, one atom or group replaces another, so there are two products.
w: In the first reaction a Br atom replaces an H atom on ethane and HBr is released: the halogenation of an alkane, a substitution. The second and fourth reactions add to a C=C (addition), and the third removes water to form a C=C (elimination, dehydration).
x: Here HBr adds across a C=C and only one product forms. That is an addition (hydrohalogenation).
Here an alcohol loses H<sub>2</sub>O and a C=C forms. That is an elimination (dehydration).
Here H<sub>2</sub> adds across a C=C. That is an addition (hydrogenation).

q: A cyclohexane ring carries a sec-butyl group. Which drawing shows this compound, sec-butylcyclohexane?
h: A sec-butyl group attaches to the ring through a carbon that is bonded to two other carbons (one CH<sub>3</sub> and one CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>).
w: In sec-butyl the attachment carbon is "secondary": it carries one methyl and one ethyl group, –CH(CH3)CH2CH3. The straight four-carbon chain is butyl; the Y-shaped group attached through a CH2 is isobutyl; the carbon bearing three methyls is tert-butyl.
x: This is butyl, the straight four-carbon chain attached through its end carbon. Sec-butyl attaches through an inner carbon.
This is isobutyl: attached through a CH<sub>2</sub> that leads to a Y-shaped CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>. The attachment carbon here is bonded to only one other carbon in the group.
This is tert-butyl: the attachment carbon carries three CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Sec-butyl's attachment carbon is bonded to two carbons in the group.

q: In 2-methylbutane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, how is carbon 2 (the carbon that carries the CH<sub>3</sub> branch) classified?
h: Count how many other carbon atoms are bonded directly to carbon 2.
w: Carbon 2 is bonded to C1, C3 and the CH3 branch: three other carbons, so it is tertiary (3°). A carbon's class counts carbon neighbors only; the H atoms do not count.
x: A secondary carbon is bonded to two other carbons. Carbon 2 also carries the CH<sub>3</sub> branch, so count again.
A primary carbon is bonded to only one other carbon, like the CH<sub>3</sub> groups at the ends of the chain. Carbon 2 is in the middle and is branched.
A quaternary carbon is bonded to four other carbons and has no H. Carbon 2 still has one H.

q: Which alkane contains a quaternary (4°) carbon?
h: A quaternary carbon is bonded to four other carbons, so it has no H atoms at all. Look for a C with two branches on it.
w: In 2,2-dimethylbutane, carbon 2 carries two CH3 branches and is also bonded to C1 and C3: four carbons, no H. So 2,2-dimethylbutane has a quaternary carbon. All four compounds are C6H14 isomers.
x: Carbon 2 of 2-methylpentane has one branch and one H, so it is bonded to three carbons: tertiary, not quaternary.
Carbon 3 of 3-methylpentane has one branch and one H, so it is tertiary. A quaternary carbon needs two branches on the same carbon.
Hexane is unbranched. Its end carbons are primary and its inner carbons are secondary; none is bonded to four carbons.

q: How many secondary (2°) carbons are in 3-methylhexane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: A secondary carbon is bonded to exactly two other carbons. In an alkane, that is every CH<sub>2</sub> in the chain.
w: Classify each carbon: the three CH3 groups are 1°, the CH carrying the branch (C3) is 3°, and the three CH2 groups (C2, C4, C5) are 2°. There are 3 secondary carbons.
x: Two misses one of the CH<sub>2</sub> groups. There are CH<sub>2</sub> groups at C2, C4 and C5.
Four counts C3 as secondary, but C3 is bonded to C2, C4 and the CH<sub>3</sub> branch: three carbons, so it is tertiary.
One counts only a single CH<sub>2</sub>. Every CH<sub>2</sub> inside the chain is bonded to two carbons.

q: Under which conditions does an alkane such as methane react with Cl<sub>2</sub>?
c: when the mixture is heated or exposed to light (UV)
in the dark at room temperature, with no catalyst
with H<sub>2</sub> and a platinum catalyst
with water and an acid catalyst
h: Alkanes are unreactive. What energy source starts their reaction with a halogen?
w: Alkanes have only strong, nonpolar C–C and C–H bonds, so a halogen reacts with them only when heat or light supplies energy. A Cl atom then replaces an H (a substitution), and HCl forms.
x: In the dark at room temperature an alkane and Cl<sub>2</sub> do not react. That is why the reaction needs a source of energy.
H<sub>2</sub> with a Pt catalyst is the condition for hydrogenating an alkene. An alkane has no C=C to add H<sub>2</sub> to.
Water and an acid catalyst hydrate an alkene. Alkanes do not react with water.

q: When methane reacts with excess Cl<sub>2</sub> in light, the products include CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>, CHCl<sub>3</sub> (chloroform, once used as an anesthetic) and CCl<sub>4</sub>, not just CH<sub>3</sub>Cl. Why do these more highly chlorinated products form?
c: CH<sub>3</sub>Cl still has C–H bonds, so a Cl can replace another H, and then another
Cl<sub>2</sub> adds across a C=C that forms in methane
CCl<sub>4</sub> forms first and then loses Cl atoms one at a time
Methane molecules join into a polymer that contains chlorine
h: Halogenation is a substitution: one Cl replaces one H. How many H atoms does CH<sub>3</sub>Cl still have?
w: Each substitution replaces one H with one Cl and releases HCl. CH3Cl still has three C–H bonds, so with excess Cl2 further substitutions give CH2Cl2, then CHCl3, then CCl4.
x: Methane is an alkane and has no C=C. Halogenation of an alkane is a substitution, not an addition.
The reaction goes the other way: H atoms are replaced by Cl one at a time, starting from CH<sub>4</sub>.
Halogenation does not link methane molecules together. Each product still has only one carbon.

q: Propane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, reacts with Cl<sub>2</sub> in light. Counting only products with ONE Cl, how many different compounds can form?
h: Replace one H with Cl at each different kind of carbon. Are the two end carbons different from each other?
w: Cl can replace an H on an end carbon (1-chloropropane, CH3CH2CH2Cl) or on the middle carbon (2-chloropropane, CH3CHClCH3). The two end carbons are equivalent, so there are 2 monochlorinated products.
x: One counts only a single position. The middle CH<sub>2</sub> is different from the two end CH<sub>3</sub> groups.
Three counts each carbon separately, but C1 and C3 are equivalent: putting Cl on either end gives the same compound, 1-chloropropane.
Eight counts every H atom. Many H atoms are equivalent, and replacing equivalent H atoms gives the same compound.

q: Ethylene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub>, is the plant hormone that Valley packing houses use to ripen fruit. It is also the monomer of polyethylene, used in plastic bags and squeeze bottles. How does polyethylene form?
c: Addition polymerization: each C=C opens and the monomers join into a long chain of –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– units
Condensation polymerization: each pair of monomers joins and gives off a water molecule
Substitution: a Cl atom replaces an H atom on each ethylene molecule
Combustion: ethylene reacts with O<sub>2</sub> to give a long chain
h: Ethylene has a C=C and no O or N atoms. Which kind of reaction lets alkenes link to each other without losing any atoms?
w: In addition polymerization, the double bond of each alkene monomer opens and the carbons bond to the next monomer, giving a chain of repeating –CH2–CH2– units. No atoms are lost, so the polymer has the same formula ratio as the monomer.
x: Condensation polymers such as nylon and polyesters form from monomers with –COOH, –OH or –NH<sub>2</sub> groups, which lose water. Ethylene has no such groups.
Replacing H with Cl would be a substitution and would not link monomers together. PVC is made from a monomer that already contains Cl.
Combustion breaks a hydrocarbon down to CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O. It does not build chains.

q: Polypropylene is the plastic in most disposable syringe barrels. Which monomer is used to make it?
h: An addition polymer is named after its monomer, and the monomer must have a C=C.
w: Polypropylene is made by addition polymerization of propene, CH2=CHCH3. Each C=C opens, and the CH3 groups hang off every other carbon of the chain.
x: Propane has no C=C, so it cannot undergo addition polymerization.
Ethene is the monomer of polyethylene. Polypropylene has a CH<sub>3</sub> branch on every other carbon, so its monomer has three carbons.
Chloroethene (vinyl chloride) is the monomer of PVC, the plastic in IV bags. Polypropylene contains no chlorine.

q: Teflon, the nonstick coating, is the addition polymer of tetrafluoroethene, CF<sub>2</sub>=CF<sub>2</sub>. Which is its repeating unit?
h: In addition polymerization the C=C becomes a single bond, and every atom of the monomer stays in the polymer.
w: The double bond opens to link monomers, so the repeating unit is –CF2–CF2–, with only single bonds and all four F atoms kept.
x: A carbon with a C=C and two F atoms could not also bond to the next unit. The C=C becomes a single bond as the chain forms.
This unit has H atoms, but the monomer has none. Each carbon keeps its two F atoms.
A CF<sub>3</sub> carbon has only one bond left, so it could end a chain but cannot be a repeating unit in the middle.

q: On cold Valley nights, a gas wall heater or a generator burning fuel with too little air produces a deadly, odorless gas. Incomplete combustion of a hydrocarbon forms which product that complete combustion does not?
h: Complete combustion gives CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O. What forms when there is not enough O<sub>2</sub> to finish the job?
w: With too little O2, some carbon is only partly oxidized and leaves as carbon monoxide, CO. CO binds the iron in hemoglobin far more tightly than O2 does, which is why fuel-burning devices must never be run indoors.
x: CO<sub>2</sub> is the product of complete combustion.
Water forms in both complete and incomplete combustion.
O<sub>2</sub> is a reactant in combustion, not a product.

q: Which condensed formula is 2-hexene (hex-2-ene)?
h: The stem gives the number of carbons in the chain. The number tells you which carbon the double bond starts on.
w: Hex- means a six-carbon chain and 2- means the double bond starts at carbon 2, between C2 and C3: CH3CH=CHCH2CH2CH3.
x: Here the double bond starts at the first carbon of the chain, so this is 1-hexene.
Here the double bond is between C3 and C4, in the middle of the chain, so this is 3-hexene.
The double bond is in the right place, but count the carbons: there are only five. This is 2-pentene.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Count the carbons in the chain, then number from the end that reaches the double bond first.
w: The chain has seven carbons (hept-). Numbering from the right end reaches the double bond at carbon 2, the lowest possible number, so the name is 2-heptene (hept-2-ene).
x: This numbers the chain from the left end. The chain must be numbered from the end nearer the double bond, which gives 2 instead of 5.
Count again: there are seven carbons, including both CH carbons of the double bond. Hex- would mean six.
The ending -yne is for a C≡C triple bond. This compound has a C=C double bond, so the ending is -ene.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub>?
h: When a chain has both a double bond and a branch, which one decides the direction of numbering?
w: The longest chain containing the double bond has five carbons. The double bond has priority, so number from the right: the double bond is at C1 and the methyl group lands on C4, giving 4-methyl-1-pentene (4-methylpent-1-ene).
x: This numbers from the left to give the methyl group the lower number. The double bond gets the lowest number, even if that gives the branch a higher one.
1-Hexene is an unbranched six-carbon chain. Here the longest chain is five carbons, and the sixth carbon is a methyl branch.
The ending -ane is for a compound with only single bonds. The C=C must appear in the name as -ene, and it also sets the numbering.

q: Which condensed formula is 3-methyl-1-butene (3-methylbut-1-ene)?
h: Write a four-carbon chain, put the double bond where the name says, then number from that end to place the methyl group.
w: But-1-ene is a four-carbon chain with the double bond between C1 and C2. A methyl group on C3 gives CH2=CHCH(CH3)CH3.
x: Here the methyl group is on C2, one of the double-bond carbons. This is 2-methyl-1-butene.
Here the double bond is between C2 and C3 and the methyl group is on C2. This is 2-methyl-2-butene.
The double bond and the methyl group are at the right numbers, but the chain has five carbons. This is 3-methyl-1-pentene.

q: A hydrocarbon is a ring of five carbon atoms with one C=C double bond in the ring and no branches. What is its name?
h: Build the name from three parts: one for the ring, one for the number of carbons and one for the double bond.
w: Cyclo- means a ring, pent- means five carbons and -ene means a C=C double bond: cyclopentene, C5H8.
x: Cyclopentane is the five-carbon ring with only single bonds. The double bond changes the ending from -ane to -ene.
1-Pentene is an open chain of five carbons with a double bond. A ring needs the prefix cyclo-.
Hex- means six carbons. This ring has five, so the stem is pent-.

q: Which condensed formula is 2-pentyne (pent-2-yne)?
h: The ending tells you the kind of multiple bond, the stem tells you the chain length and the number tells you where the multiple bond starts.
w: Pent- is five carbons, -yne is a C≡C triple bond and 2- puts it between C2 and C3: CH3C≡CCH2CH3. The triple-bond carbons carry no hydrogens here because each already has four bonds.
x: Here the triple bond starts at the first carbon of the chain, so this is 1-pentyne.
This has a C=C double bond, so it is 2-pentene. The ending -yne means a triple bond.
The triple bond is at C2, but the chain has six carbons. This is 2-hexyne.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Find the longest continuous chain, number it from the end nearer the branches, and give each branch its own number.
w: The longest chain has six carbons (hexane). Numbering from the left puts both CH3 groups on carbon 3, and each one needs a number: 3,3-dimethylhexane.
x: This numbers the chain from the right end. Numbering from the left reaches the branches sooner (carbon 3 instead of carbon 4), and the lower number is used.
Each substituent needs its own number, even when two are on the same carbon. Two methyl groups on carbon 3 are written 3,3-dimethyl.
This uses a five-carbon chain and treats two chain carbons as an ethyl branch. The longest continuous chain has six carbons, so the parent is hexane.

q: Which condensed formula is 2,3-dimethylpentane?
h: Write the parent chain from the last part of the name, number it, then hang one group on each numbered carbon.
w: Pentane is a five-carbon chain. One CH3 goes on carbon 2 and one on carbon 3, which gives CH3CH(CH3)CH(CH3)CH2CH3.
x: Here the methyl groups are on carbons 2 and 4 of the five-carbon chain. This is 2,4-dimethylpentane.
Here both methyl groups are on carbon 2. This is 2,2-dimethylpentane; the name asked for has one on carbon 2 and one on carbon 3.
The branches are on carbons 2 and 3, but the chain has only four carbons. This is 2,3-dimethylbutane.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH(CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: After you number the chain, put the substituent names in alphabetical order. Do prefixes such as di- and tri- count when you alphabetize?
w: The longest chain has seven carbons. Numbering from the left gives branches at 2, 3 and 4. Ethyl comes before methyl in the alphabet (the di- is ignored), so the name is 4-ethyl-2,3-dimethylheptane.
x: The numbers are right, but substituents are listed in alphabetical order, not number order. The prefix di- is ignored, so ethyl (e) comes before methyl (m).
This numbers the chain from the right end. Numbering from the left gives 2, 3, 4, which is lower than 4, 5, 6.
Two methyl groups need the prefix di-. Two numbers followed by plain "methyl" is not a complete name.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: The longest chain does not have to be the one written in a straight line. Try counting through the group in parentheses.
w: The longest chain runs through the CH2CH3 group: two carbons, the CH, then three more, for six carbons (hexane). The leftover CH3 is on carbon 3, so the name is 3-methylhexane.
x: This takes the chain as written (five carbons) and calls the CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> a branch. Counting through that group gives a longer, six-carbon chain, and the longest chain must be the parent.
The parent chain is right, but it is numbered from the wrong end. Start from the end nearer the branch, which puts the methyl group on carbon 3.
This picks a four-carbon chain and calls the rest a propyl branch. The parent must be the longest continuous chain, which has six carbons.

q: What is the molecular formula of 3-ethyl-2-methylpentane?
h: Add the carbons in the parent chain to the carbons in each substituent. Then use the general formula for an alkane to get the hydrogens.
w: Pentane gives 5 carbons, the ethyl group 2 and the methyl group 1, for 8 carbons. An alkane is CnH2n+2, so the formula is C8H18.
x: C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> counts only the parent chain, pentane. The carbons in the ethyl and methyl branches are part of the molecule as well.
C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> counts each branch as one carbon. An ethyl group has two carbons, so the total is 5 + 2 + 1 = 8.
Eight carbons is right, but a branched alkane still follows C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>. Branching does not remove hydrogens, so there are 18.
